pairs.rationale: Genesis names Melchizedek king of Salem and priest of God Most High and records his blessing of Abram. Its preceding context describes the return after the kings were defeated; Hebrews explicitly describes Melchizedek meeting and blessing Abraham.

Genesis names the Salem king and records a tenth of all being given. Hebrews explicitly identifies Abraham as giver and interprets the names as righteousness and peace; those name interpretations are not printed in Genesis.

The later sequence connects priestly likeness to Melchizedek with an indestructible life and the priest-for-the-age testimony. This develops the continual-priest likeness without settling historical parentage or identifying Melchizedek personally with the Son.

Genesis records the tenth-of-all transaction after Melchizedek blesses Abram. Hebrews explicitly calls the giver Abraham the patriarch and describes choice spoils and the recipient's greatness, details not all stated in the selected Genesis sentence.

Numbers assigns Israel's tithes to sons of Levi in return for Tent service. Hebrews specifically describes those receiving the priestly office and collecting from Abrahamic brothers; those office and ancestry qualifications are not the wording of the selected Numbers verses.

Genesis records Melchizedek blessing Abram and the tenth-of-all transaction. Hebrews uses this episode to contrast the recipient with the Levitical line and to identify Abraham as the promise holder; Genesis does not state that full genealogical argument here.

The preceding verse names the blessing of the promise holder by the non-Levitical tithe recipient. The source states the lesser-and-greater principle by which that blessing is interpreted, rather than introducing a second blessing event.

The chapter contrasts mortal tithe receivers with one testified alive, then contrasts priests stopped by death with Jesus' permanent priesthood. These related contrasts develop the argument without requiring the two referents to be identical.

The following verse explains the qualified claim that Levi paid through Abraham: Levi was still in his father's loins at the meeting. The source's so-to-speak qualification remains essential; no separate attendance or payment by a living Levi is asserted.

Genesis supplies the Melchizedek-and-Abram blessing and tithe episode invoked by the source's meeting reference. Levi is not named in this Genesis passage; the ancestral participation explanation belongs to Hebrews' preceding so-to-speak argument.

Psalm 109:4 supplies the priesthood according to Melchizedek's order on which Hebrews' question turns. The Psalm states the sworn continuing priesthood; Hebrews draws the contrast with Aaron and asks about Levitical perfection.

The later passage describes setting aside the preceding commandment because the law perfected nothing and introducing a better hope. This develops the source's inference that a changed priesthood entails a change of law.
The following verse identifies the other tribe as Judah and the person as our Lord, supplying the named tribal explanation for the source's altar-service contrast.

Matthew introduces Jesus Christ's origin with a genealogical sequence naming Judah and Perez. This supplies Judah-line background; the selected opening does not make Hebrews' claim about Moses' silence concerning priests from that tribe.

The testimony about a priest for the age according to Melchizedek's order supplies the scriptural warrant for the source's other-priest likeness. The intervening verse explains the contrast in terms of indestructible life.

Romans states that the risen Christ no longer dies and death no longer rules over Him, corresponding to the indestructible-life basis described in Hebrews. Romans does not discuss priestly appointment or the fleshly commandment in this verse.

Psalm 109:4 contains the Melchizedek-order priesthood testimony. Hebrews prints for the age where the Psalm prints for ever; the source quotes the priesthood clause rather than the Psalm's complete oath sentence.

The following verse explains the weakness behind setting aside the preceding commandment: the law perfected nothing, while a better hope permits approach to God. This links the stated reason to the source's conclusion.

The later passage likewise says the law's repeatedly offered sacrifices cannot perfect those approaching. It develops the imperfection claim through sacrificial repetition, while the source also introduces the better hope for drawing near to God.

The following verse completes the contrast between priests appointed without an oath and the One addressed by the Lord's sworn priesthood declaration. The source and target are stages of one argument.

Psalm 109:4 supplies the Lord's oath and continuing priesthood. Hebrews prints will not change His mind and for the age, while the Psalm prints will not change His purpose and for ever; Hebrews omits the Melchizedek-order ending in this occurrence.

Both passages name a better covenant in relation to Jesus' priestly ministry. The source calls Him guarantor, whereas the later passage calls Him mediator and speaks of better promises; the titles are preserved as distinct.

The next verse sets the death-interrupted succession of many priests against the One who remains for the age with a permanent priesthood. It supplies the contrasting case rather than a separate death narrative.

The following therefore connects permanent priesthood and remaining for the age with saving those approaching God and always living to intercede. The link makes the source's stated permanence and its consequence explicit.

Romans likewise names Christ Jesus as risen and interceding for us, adding His place at God's right hand. Hebrews explains complete salvation for those approaching God through His always-living intercession; the formulations retain their respective emphasis.

The earlier passage names Jesus the Son of God as high priest who passed through the heavens and was tested without sin. The source describes holiness and being higher than the heavens; passed through and higher than remain distinct descriptions.

The later passage likewise contrasts daily repeated priestly sacrifices with the One's single sacrifice for sins. The source adds the own-sins-and-people distinction and explicitly identifies the once-for-all offering as Himself.

The earlier sequence connects Christ's divinely given Son and priest titles with suffering, learned obedience, and being perfected. The source summarizes the oath's appointment of a Son perfected for the age in contrast to the law's weak appointees.

The Psalm's invitation to sit at the Lord's right hand corresponds to Hebrews' right-hand enthronement language. Hebrews identifies the seated figure as our high priest and adds the heavenly throne of the Majesty; the selected Psalm sentence does not itself name the priestly office.

The source calls the sanctuary the true tent pitched by the Lord rather than a human. The later passage describes Christ's greater and more perfect tent as not made by hands and not of this creation, preserving its distinct descriptive wording.

The earlier statement likewise defines every high priest's appointment in terms of offering gifts and sacrifices, explicitly for sins. The source uses that function to infer that this One also must have something to offer.

The earlier tribal argument identifies the Lord with Judah rather than the tribe serving at the altar. This provides the legal-priesthood context for the source's earthly-priesthood counterfactual and its reference to lawful gift offerers.

Exodus supplies the command to make according to the pattern shown on the mountain. Exodus prints make them, while Hebrews prints make everything and uses the instruction to explain the copy-and-shadow service.

Both passages name a better covenant in connection with Jesus' priestly role. The source calls Him mediator and mentions better promises; the earlier passage calls Him guarantor. These related titles are retained as distinct.

The source argues that seeking a second covenant implies a fault in the first. After the intervening new-covenant quotation, the target draws the related conclusion that calling it new makes the first old and aging.

Jeremiah 38:31 promises a new covenant with the houses of Israel and Judah. Hebrews prints Look and conclude where Jeremiah prints Behold and make, and adds the introductory finding-fault clause before the quotation.

Both passages contrast the promised covenant with the fathers' exodus covenant and say they did not remain in it and the Lord disregarded them. Their hand-taking and leading-out phrases differ slightly; the supplied Greek-based Jeremiah wording is preserved.

Jeremiah 38:33 supplies the promised laws within and written on hearts, followed by God-and-people belonging. Both retain My laws in the plural; Hebrews prints mind and inscribe where Jeremiah prints understanding and write.

The first part of Jeremiah 38:34 supplies the fellow-citizen-and-brother teaching contrast and knowledge of the Lord from least to greatest. The target also contains the mercy-and-sins sentence, which Hebrews places in its following verse.

The closing part of Jeremiah 38:34 supplies mercy and sins remembered no more. Hebrews prints wrongdoings where Jeremiah prints injustices; Jeremiah's same verse also contains the preceding knowledge-of-the-Lord promise.

The source explicitly reasons from the word new in the earlier new-covenant declaration. Linking that precise wording makes the new-versus-old inference visible without assigning an external date to the predicted disappearance.

Exodus commands a sanctuary and its vessels made according to the pattern shown on the mountain. These earthly construction instructions supply background for Hebrews' first-covenant sanctuary and worship regulations; Exodus does not call this covenant first in the selected passage.

Exodus places the table and bread of the Presence outside the veil and describes the lampstand and its lamps. Hebrews summarizes these furnishings as lampstand, table, and presentation of loaves in the first tent, called the Holy Place.

Exodus prescribes the veil and expressly says it divides the Holy Place from the Holy of Holies, with the ark within. Hebrews identifies the area behind the second curtain as the tent called the Holy of Holies.

Exodus describes the gold-covered incense altar and places it opposite the veil. Hebrews describes the inner tent as having a golden incense altar. The object and gold correspond, while the differing placement language is preserved rather than reconciled by changing altar to censer.

Exodus prescribes an ark overlaid with pure gold outside and inside and directs that the testimonies be put into it. This corresponds to Hebrews' gold-covered ark of the covenant; Exodus does not list all three contents named by Hebrews in this range.

Exodus names a golden jar filled with manna and directs its preservation before God and before the Testimony. Hebrews lists a golden jar of manna in its ark-content statement; before and in remain distinct placement descriptions.

Numbers 17:23-25 records Aaron's sprouted staff, its shoot, blossoms and nuts, and its preservation before the testimonies. Hebrews names the sprouted rod among the ark contents; the target's before-placement and nuts wording are preserved.

Deuteronomy explicitly says the tablets were put into the ark and remained there as commanded. This directly corresponds to the tablets named among Hebrews' ark contents; the selected Deuteronomy verse does not describe the manna jar or rod.

Exodus describes the cherubim above the ark, their wings overshadowing the cover, and the cover's placement. Hebrews briefly names this arrangement before declining detailed exposition; its atonement cover and Exodus' propitiatory cover retain their respective labels.

Exodus prescribes a continually burning lamp outside the veil, with Aaron and his sons tending its burning from evening to morning. This supplies a concrete recurring outer-tent service behind Hebrews' summary of continual priestly worship, rather than a complete list of those acts.

Leviticus describes blood brought within the veil and excludes anyone else from the tent during atonement for the officiant, his house and Israel. Hebrews summarizes the high priest's sole annual blood entry; the annual rule is also explicit in the separately read Leviticus 16:34.

The later passage describes confidence for entry in Jesus' blood through the new living way inaugurated through the curtain. This contrasts with the source's undisclosed way while the first tent stands; the Holy Spirit's indication is the source's own formulation.

The later passage likewise says repeated sacrifices cannot perfect those approaching and reasons about worshipers' consciousness of sins. Hebrews 9:9 specifies perfection with respect to conscience; consciousness of sins is retained as the later wording.

Colossians likewise connects eating and drinking disputes with shadow language and Christ, while also naming festivals, new moons and Sabbaths. Hebrews names foods, drinks and washings as time-limited fleshly regulations; the settings and complete lists are not equated.

The earlier passage describes the true tent pitched by the Lord rather than a human. The source describes Christ's greater and more perfect tent, not made by hands and not of this creation; its good things that have come to be is retained without being changed to a future expression.

Both emphasize once-for-all efficacy: the source describes entry through His own blood and eternal redemption, while the later passage describes sanctification through the offering of Jesus Christ's body. Blood, body, redemption and sanctification retain their respective formulations.

Leviticus describes sprinkling calf's blood and the male young goat's blood at the propitiatory cover in the holy-place atonement rite. Hebrews speaks of goats and bulls and fleshly cleanness; this is sacrificial-blood background, not identical animal-label or cleansing-object wording.

Numbers prescribes keeping the heifer's ashes for water of sprinkling as a means of purification, corresponding to Hebrews' heifer-ash cleansing example. The separately read Numbers 19:17-19 describes ashes mixed with living water and sprinkling people, distinguishing this from the blood rite.

Both describe Christ's blood with unblemished sacrificial imagery. Peter describes ransom from ancestral futile conduct; Hebrews describes His self-offering through an eternal Spirit to God and cleansing conscience from dead works for service. These agency and benefit formulations remain distinct.

Jesus' cup saying names the new covenant in His blood poured out for you. Hebrews names the new-covenant mediator and death for redemption under the first covenant, adding eternal inheritance; the single Luke verse does not state that full inheritance argument.

The following sentence explains the death requirement by the testament taking effect at death rather than while its maker lives. These are joined stages of Hebrews' own argument; the link does not add an independent legal code.

The preceding sentence introduces the requirement that the testament maker's death be established; the source gives the death-versus-living explanation. The English testament terminology is retained rather than silently replacing it with the surrounding covenant terminology.

Exodus records covenant blood assigned to the altar and sprinkled over the people, with the covenant book read aloud. This supplies the inauguration narrative behind Hebrews' statement that even the first covenant was not inaugurated without blood.

Exodus records calves, blood at the altar and over the people, and the covenant book being read. Hebrews additionally specifies goats, water, scarlet wool, hyssop, and sprinkling the book itself; the selected Exodus passage does not report all those features.

Exodus supplies Moses' blood-of-the-covenant declaration. Hebrews prints This is and God commanded for you, while Exodus prints Behold and the Lord has made with you concerning all these words; the two formulations are not treated as verbally identical.

Leviticus names Moses, the tent and utensils in consecration with anointing oil, including sprinkling the altar and anointing the tent. Hebrews specifies blood sprinkled on the tent and ministry vessels. This compares sanctuary consecration while preserving the differing material and action-object wording.

Leviticus gives blood upon the altar for atonement in place of life. Hebrews connects lawful cleansing and forgiveness with blood, retaining its almost-everything qualifier for cleansing and its separate statement about shedding blood and forgiveness.

The earlier copy-and-shadow description identifies the earthly service patterned on heavenly things. Hebrews 9:23 develops that distinction through cleansing copies and better sacrifices for heavenly things; the earlier target does not itself describe heavenly cleansing.

Romans locates the risen Christ at God's right hand interceding for us. Hebrews describes Christ entering heaven itself to appear before God's face on our behalf; the shared representation theme retains the distinct place and action formulations.

Leviticus expressly commands atonement for Israel once in the year. Hebrews uses the high priest's yearly entry with another's blood as the contrast to Christ's not entering to offer Himself repeatedly; the statutory pattern and Christ's action are distinct.

The later passage likewise describes one sacrifice for sins for all time rather than daily repetition. The source describes appearing once at the end of the ages through His sacrifice; its temporal phrase is not replaced with the target's for-all-time wording.

Both state the prospect of judgment. Corinthians specifies Christ's judgment seat and recompense for what each has done through the body; Hebrews also orders death then judgment, an order not expressly stated in the selected Corinthians verse.

Isaiah describes the one delivered to death as bearing the sins of many and being delivered up for their sins. Hebrews applies sin-bearing language to Christ's once offering, then adds His second appearance for awaiting people; the selected Isaiah verse does not state that second appearance.

Philippians describes eagerly awaiting the Savior, the Lord Jesus Christ, from the heavens. This corresponds to Hebrews' awaiting-Christ salvation expectation; Hebrews additionally specifies His second appearance apart from sin, which the selected Philippians verse does not state.

distinctions: Genesis uses Abram and pronoun forms where Hebrews explicitly names Abraham as tenth giver; Genesis name interpretations are not supplied by its narrative.
Melchizedek likeness, lineage, mortality and permanent-priesthood arguments are not treated as independent historical biography or personal identity proof.
Numbers assigns tithes to sons of Levi; Hebrews specifies priestly office and Abrahamic brothers.
Psalm 109:4 native numbering and differences in age/for ever and mind/purpose wording preserved.
Guarantor and mediator, and higher than versus passed through the heavens, remain distinct.
Psalm 109 native numbering; right-hand language is linked without treating the selected Psalm sentence as naming the high-priest office.
Jeremiah 38:31-34, not conventional Hebrew chapter 31; laws plural and mind/understanding, inscribe/write, wrongdoings/injustices differences kept.
Exodus 25:40 them and Hebrews everything; guarantor and mediator remain distinct.
The new/old inference is internal textual reasoning, without importing a historical disappearance date.
Hebrews golden incense altar retained as altar, with Exodus opposite-veil wording; manna jar and rod before-Testimony descriptions not normalized to Hebrews in-it wording.
Native Numbers 17:23-25 has sprouted rod and nuts; Deuteronomy 10:5 explicitly places tablets in ark.
Hebrews eternal Spirit, have-come-to-be, testament, almost, once-for-all and second-appearance wording retained.
Exodus 24 additional and differing details, and Leviticus 8 oil/anointing versus Hebrews blood/sprinkling, explicitly distinguished.
Psalm/OT native numbering, atonement/propitiatory cover labels, animal labels, and conscience/consciousness wording preserved.
